docs.title: HSBcad Documentation
docs.text:
Welcome to the community knowledge base for HSBcad, the Revit add-in for timber frame construction.

HSBcad's official tutorials are published as YouTube videos. This site turns each video into a written, searchable page with:

  • An embedded video you can watch in place
  • A clickable chapter list that jumps straight to the right moment
  • A step-by-step walkthrough with exact ribbon paths, panel names, and parameter values
  • A glossary of HSBcad-specific terms used in the video

docs.title: Start here
docs.text:
• Browse the full list in Videos.
  • Look up any HSBcad-specific term in the Glossary.
  • Use the search bar at the top to find a feature, command, or term.
  • Toggle dark mode with the sun/moon icon in the top right.

docs.title: About this project
docs.text: This wiki is built with MkDocs Material and hosted on GitHub Pages. The source lives at BeterGevel/Revit_HSBCAD_documentation; maintainer documentation is in CONTRIBUTING.md.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
Canonical definitions for HSBcad and Revit terms used across this wiki. Every video page links its terms here so definitions stay consistent.

When a new term is introduced in a tutorial that isn't listed here yet, it appears as a glossary-add comment in the draft. Promote it to this file before publishing the video page.

docs.title: Alias
docs.text: A named placeholder defined in a framing style that maps to a specific Revit material or beam size. Aliases let you describe a framing style abstractly ("the stud material", "the sheathing material") and swap the underlying material in one place.

docs.title: Framing styles editor
docs.text: The interface in HSBcad where wall framing styles and their connection details are defined. Open it from the HSBcad ribbon.

docs.title: Framing style
docs.text: A reusable template that defines the structure of a wall — the layout of its studs, plates, sheets, and other elements. Walls in the model are built from one or more framing styles.

docs.title: Detail
docs.text: A reusable connection design defined inside a framing style — for example a corner detail, an edge detail, or a junction between two framing styles. Details are parametric and can be reused across the model.

docs.title: Preview style
docs.text: A temporary visual setting inside the Framing styles editor that lets you preview how a detail adapts to different wall thicknesses or framing styles. Changing the preview style affects visualisation only, not the saved detail.

docs.title: Offset line
docs.text: A reference line inside a detail used to align and anchor elements. Offset lines can be parametric so the distance they represent (for example, the gap between two walls) can be controlled by a parameter.

docs.title: Anchor / anchoring
docs.text: The act of locking an element in a detail to a reference (an offset line, another element, or the boundary of a sheet) so its position updates automatically when the reference changes. Anchored elements stay in the correct place when the wall thickness or other parameters change.

docs.title: Beam code
docs.text: A short code (for example CD, CDS) assigned to elements in a detail to identify their type or function. Beam codes are used downstream by the construction generator and by reporting.

docs.title: Element inventory
docs.text: A library of predefined beams and sheets you can insert into a framing style or detail. Each framing style has its own inventory of default beams that you can pull from.

docs.title: Free inventory item
docs.text: An element added manually to a detail (rather than from the framing style's predefined inventory) that exposes instance parameters so its dimensions can be adjusted per detail. Commonly used for OSB sheets and trim pieces.

docs.title: Instance parameter
docs.text: A property of an element — like width, height, or visibility — that can be adjusted per instance, usually by dragging an edge or editing a value in the parameter panel.

docs.title: Distance parameter
docs.text: A user-defined parameter that stores a length value (for example, the size of a gap). Distance parameters can be referenced by offset lines and element dimensions to make a detail fully parametric.

docs.title: Yes/No parameter
docs.text: A user-defined boolean parameter used to toggle elements or behaviours in a detail on and off. A common pattern is to drive an element's width with a yes/no parameter so the element disappears when toggled off.

docs.title: Connector beam
docs.text: A beam in a connection detail that bridges two framing styles — typically used to mechanically tie wall structures together at a corner or junction.

docs.title: Generate
docs.text: The HSBcad command that applies the current framing styles and details to the selected model elements and produces the actual timber-frame construction. Found on the HSBcad ribbon.

docs.title: Construction
docs.text: The set of framed wall elements (studs, plates, sheets, connectors) produced by the Generate command from a framing style or details.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: A named, saved snapshot of all parameter values inside a detail. Configurations let you switch between design variants of the same detail (for example, single-plate vs. double-plate) without rebuilding the detail from scratch — you create one detail, then save several configurations that toggle its parameters.

docs.title: Cut
docs.text: An auxiliary geometry tool inside a detail that stretches or trims an element (a beam or sheet) by targeting its beam code. Most commonly used in edge details so the sheathing sheet extends up to the top plate and down to the bottom plate.

docs.title: Edge detail
docs.text: A detail that handles what happens at the top and bottom of a sheet within a framing style — for example, ensuring an OSB sheet extends all the way to the wall boundaries.

docs.title: Zone
docs.text: A distinct spatial layer within a wall framing style — for example the structural stud core, exterior sheathing, or interior sheathing. Zones stack from interior to exterior and are numbered relative to the core (Zone 0): positive numbers face outward, negative numbers face inward.

docs.title: Zone filler
docs.text: The logic that determines how a zone is populated when the wall is generated — most commonly Beam Distribution (which lays out studs at a configurable spacing) or Sheet Distribution (which lays out sheathing panels). Each zone has exactly one filler.

docs.title: Rely on
docs.text: A zone setting that forces the filler of one zone to align with the splits or elements of another zone. Typically used so the structural studs in Zone 0 align with the vertical seams of the sheathing in an adjacent zone.

docs.title: Item container
docs.text: A logical boundary placed on a Revit wall that tells HSBcad which portion of the wall to frame. Item containers are the unit of selection for Generate, lock, and renumber operations — without one on a wall, HSBcad cannot produce a construction for it.

docs.title: Model group
docs.text: A named collection of item containers that can be managed, filtered, or generated together as a single unit — useful for grouping all walls of one storey or one building section.

docs.title: Match framing styles
docs.text: The HSBcad command that links Revit wall types to specific framing styles, including alignment (interior, center, exterior) and offset. The mapping is saved with the project so newly drawn walls of those types pick up the right framing automatically.

docs.title: Presenter jargon
docs.text: These are informal terms presenters use in the videos. They are translated to the approved UI vocabulary in tutorial steps; the originals live here as a translation aid.

docs.title: Snatch
docs.text: Drag the cursor onto a reference line or point until it highlights, then release to anchor the element to that reference. Translated to "drag … onto" in tutorial steps.

docs.title: Hit
docs.text: Click a button or invoke a command. Translated to "click" in tutorial steps.

docs.title: Videos
docs.text:
All HSBcad tutorial videos that have been transcribed into written pages. Click any title to open the full walkthrough with chapter timestamps.

  • Complex connection details — Create a parametric corner detail with an OSB sheet and a toggleable connector beam.
  • Define custom wall framing styles — Build exterior and interior wall framing styles from scratch in the Framing Styles Editor.
  • Stretching wall sheets using edge details — Use edge details and the Cut tool to extend OSB sheets all the way to the top and bottom plates, with configurations to toggle a second base plate.
  • Match framing styles and generate item containers — Link Revit walls to framing styles, place and number item containers, then generate the 3D timber construction.

docs.title: Create complex connection details for exterior walls
docs.text:
Video info

Source: Watch on YouTube Duration: 04:28 Level: Intermediate

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: This tutorial shows how to create a parametric gap between two exterior walls in a corner connection. You will learn how to anchor elements to an offset line, add an OSB sheet with instance parameters, and control the gap and connector beam visibility using custom parameters.

docs.title: What you'll build
docs.text: A wall connection detail named corner with a parametric 5 mm gap between two framing styles, an optional OSB sheet on the outside, and a no connector toggle that hides the connector beam.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Knowledge: Basic understanding of the framing styles editor.
  • Project state: A Revit project with at least two exterior wall framing styles defined.

docs.title: Key concepts
docs.text:
• Framing styles editor — The interface where wall framing styles and connection details are defined.
  • Preview style — A temporary visual setting in the editor that lets you test how your detail adapts to different wall thicknesses.
  • Offset line — A reference line used to align and anchor elements within a detail.
  • Beam code — A code (like CD or CDS) assigned to elements to identify their type or function.
  • Element inventory — A library of predefined beams and sheets you can insert into a detail.
  • Free inventory item — An element like an OSB sheet that can be added manually to a detail and customized with instance parameters.
  • Instance parameters — Properties of an element (like width or height) that can be adjusted individually by dragging its edges.

docs.title: Chapters
docs.text: Time What you'll do 0:00 Set up the connection detail 1:26 Add the OSB sheet 2:47 Create parameters for the gap and connector 3:48 Generate and verify the construction

docs.title: Set up the connection detail (0:00)
docs.text:
Goal: Create a new detail and anchor the primary and secondary wall elements to an offset line.

Steps:

  1. Click Framing styles editor → the editor window appears.
  2. Click Connections → the connections tab opens.
  3. Select an existing exterior wall framing style → the style's details appear.
  4. Click Add detail → a new detail is created.
  5. Drag all items of the secondary wall to the left → the items move, making it easier to select points for the offset line.
  6. Drag the offset line to the outside of the sheet → the line moves to the new position.
  7. Drag the items of the secondary wall to the offset line and click the anchor icon → the items are locked to the line.
  8. Type CD in the Beam code field → the beam code updates.
  9. Drag the primary framing style to the top → the sheet moves to the top of the outside of the sheet.
  10. Type CD in the Beam code field for the primary framing style → the beam code updates.
  11. Select the connector beam and drag it to turn it → the beam rotates.
  12. Click the anchor icon on the connector beam → the beam is locked in place.
  13. Type CD in the Beam code field → the beam code updates.
  14. Select Default beam from the Element inventory for the secondary framing style → the beam updates to the larger size.

Verify: You see the primary and secondary wall elements anchored to the offset line with their beam codes updated.

Tip

Moving all items of the secondary wall to the left makes it easier to drag the offset line to the correct position.

docs.title: Add the OSB sheet (1:26)
docs.text:
Goal: Insert a free inventory item for the OSB sheet and adjust its size.

Steps:

  1. Click Add free inventory item → a new item appears in the detail.
  2. Select OSB from the item type list → the item updates to an OSB sheet, enabling instance parameters.
  3. Drag the edges of the OSB sheet to the right size → the sheet resizes.
  4. Click the anchor icon on the OSB sheet → the sheet is locked in place.
  5. Type CDS in the Beam code field → the beam code updates.
  6. Type corner in the Detail name field → the detail is renamed.

Verify: The OSB sheet is sized correctly, anchored in place, and the detail is named corner.

docs.title: Create parameters for the gap and connector (2:47)
docs.text:
Goal: Define parameters to control the gap width and the visibility of the connector beam.

Steps:

  1. Click Add parameter → a new parameter is created.
  2. Type gap for the name and select Distance for the type → the parameter is defined.
  3. Type 5 mm in the value field → the gap distance is set.
  4. Click Add parameter → another parameter is created.
  5. Type no connector for the name and select Yes/No for the type → the parameter is defined.
  6. Select the connector beam and type 0 in the Width field → the width is set to zero.
  7. Click the parameter button next to the width and select no connector → the beam width becomes parametric.
  8. Select the offset line and click the parameter button → a parameter list appears.
  9. Select gap → the offset line becomes parametric.
  10. Click OK → the detail is saved and appears in the list.
  11. Select a different framing style in the Preview style dropdown → the visualization updates to show how the parametric dimensions adapt.
  12. Click OK → the framing styles editor closes.

Verify: The detail is saved, and changing the preview style confirms that the parametric dimensions are well defined.

docs.title: Generate and verify the construction (3:48)
docs.text:
Goal: Apply the new detail to the building model and verify the result.

Steps:

  1. Select the whole building in the Revit model → the building elements are highlighted.
  2. Click Generate → the framing is rebuilt using the new detail.
  3. Click the right-side 3D view → the wall connections are visible.

Verify: You see the 5 mm parametric gap between the walls in the 3D view.

Warning

The OSB sheet on the outside might not extend all the way to the top and bottom. This is expected and will be addressed using edge details.

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text: • Not moving the secondary wall items out of the way first — this makes it difficult to select the correct points for the offset line.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text: • Address edge details so the OSB sheet extends fully to the top and bottom of the wall (covered in a follow-up tutorial).

docs.title: HSBcad terms used
docs.text:
• Beam code — A code (like CD or CDS) assigned to elements to identify their type or function.
  • Element inventory — A library of predefined beams and sheets you can insert into a detail.
  • Framing styles editor — The interface where wall framing styles and connection details are defined.
  • Free inventory item — An element like an OSB sheet that can be added manually to a detail and customized with instance parameters.
  • Instance parameters — Properties of an element (like width or height) that can be adjusted individually by dragging its edges.
  • Offset line — A reference line used to align and anchor elements within a detail.
  • Preview style — A temporary visual setting in the editor that lets you test how your detail adapts to different wall thicknesses.
  • snatch — drag the cursor onto a reference line or point until it highlights, then release to anchor.
  • hit — click a button or command.

docs.title: Key quotes
docs.text: "Because by doing so, you make it easier for yourself to snatch the points afterwards for your offset line." — 0:49

docs.title: Define custom wall framing styles
docs.text:
Video info

Source: Watch on YouTube Duration: 9:38 Level: Beginner

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: You will learn how to use the Framing Styles Editor to create custom wall templates from scratch. Setting up proper framing styles allows you to define exact material layers, stud spacings, and sheet distributions so your timber-frame walls generate accurately in the model.

docs.title: What you'll build
docs.text: An exterior wall framing style featuring a structural stud core and continuously staggered OSB sheeting on both faces, where the studs automatically align to back up the sheet splits. You will also duplicate this style to quickly create a thinner interior wall template.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Knowledge: None.
  • Project state: A Revit project is open with the HSBcad add-in active and default families loaded.

docs.title: Key concepts
docs.text:
• Framing styles editor — The interface in HSBcad where wall framing styles and their connection details are defined. Open it from the HSBcad ribbon.
  • Framing style — A reusable template that defines the structure of a wall — the layout of its studs, plates, sheets, and other elements. Walls in the model are built from one or more framing styles.
  • Beam code — A short code (for example CD, CDS) assigned to elements in a detail to identify their type or function. Beam codes are used downstream by the construction generator and by reporting.
  • Instance parameter — A property of an element — like width, height, or visibility — that can be adjusted per instance, usually by dragging an edge or editing a value in the parameter panel.
  • Alias — A named placeholder defined in a framing style that maps to a specific Revit material or beam size. Aliases let you describe a framing style abstractly and swap the underlying material in one place.
  • Zone — A distinct spatial layer within a wall framing style — for example the structural stud core, exterior sheathing, or interior sheathing.
  • Zone filler — The logic that determines how a zone is populated when the wall is generated — most commonly Beam Distribution (studs) or Sheet Distribution (sheathing).
  • Rely on — A zone setting that forces the filler of one zone to align with the splits or elements of another zone.

docs.title: Chapters
docs.text: Time What you'll do 0:00 Open the Framing styles editor 0:42 Define material aliases 1:13 Create a group and framing style 2:10 Configure the structural stud zone 4:47 Add exterior sheet distribution 6:51 Align studs to sheet splits 7:27 Add interior sheet distribution 8:07 Duplicate and modify for interior walls

docs.title: Open the Framing styles editor (0:00)
docs.text:
Goal: Access the interface where you build and manage wall templates.

Steps:

  1. Click Framing Styles Editor in the HSBcad ribbon → the Framing Styles Editor dialog opens.

Verify: The editor window appears, showing tabs for Aliases and Framing Style on the left.

docs.title: Define material aliases (0:42)
docs.text:
Goal: Create shorthand names for materials so you can easily assign them to different zones later.

Steps:

  1. Select Aliases in the left sidebar → the alias configuration panel appears.
  2. Click Add Alias → a new alias row is added.
  3. Type Studs into the text field → the alias is renamed.
  4. Click Add Alias again and type Plywood → a second alias is created.
  5. Click Add Alias again and type OSB → a third alias is created.

Verify: You see three aliases named Studs, Plywood, and OSB in the list.

docs.title: Create a group and framing style (1:13)
docs.text:
Goal: Organize your templates and create the foundational container for an exterior wall.

Steps:

  1. Select Framing Style in the left sidebar → the inventory and group tree appears.
  2. Click Add Group → a new group appears in the tree.
  3. Select Wall - Exterior Walls from the group type dropdown → the group is categorized for exterior walls.
  4. Click Add framing style inside the new group → a new style template appears.
  5. Type E1 - OSB_Stud184_OSB in the Name field → the style is renamed.
  6. Type OSB_38x184_OSB in the Description field → the description is logged.
  7. Select OSB for the OSB alias, Plywood for the Plywood alias, and 38x184 for the Studs alias in the Inventory mapping panel → the physical materials are mapped to your aliases.

Verify: The E1 framing style is listed under the Wall - Exterior Walls group with its materials mapped in the inventory.

docs.title: Configure the structural stud zone (2:10)
docs.text:
Goal: Define the main load-bearing core layer, including stud spacing and beam codes.

Steps:

  1. Click the Zones tab → the visual configuration for the wall zones appears with Zone 0 (the core layer) already created.
  2. Select Beam Distribution Filler from the Zone filler dropdown → the beam distribution properties load on the right.
  3. Select Studs from the Material dropdown → the 38x184 stud material is applied to the zone.
  4. Type 610 in the Spacing/Beam field → the stud spacing updates.
  5. Type ST in the BeamCode field → the studs receive the "ST" identifier.
  6. Select Left from the Start distribution dropdown → the studs align their spacing from the left side of the wall.
  7. Click the Inventory tab to return to the material list → the inventory list appears.
  8. Select 38x184 from the Default Beam dropdown → the top and bottom plates update to perfectly match your stud depth.

Verify: In the visual preview at the bottom, the bottom plate aligns cleanly with the vertical studs without any offsets.

docs.title: Add exterior sheet distribution (4:47)
docs.text:
Goal: Apply an outer layer of OSB sheathing that automatically minimizes waste.

Steps:

  1. Click the Zones tab → the zone editor appears.
  2. Click the + (add zone) button above Zone 0 → Zone 1 is created on the exterior side.
  3. Select Sheet Distribution from the Zone filler dropdown → the sheeting properties appear.
  4. Select OSB from the Material dropdown → the OSB sheeting is applied.
  5. Type 12 in the Thickness field → the sheet depth updates.
  6. Check the Continuously staggered box in the Distribution panel → the sheet layout adjusts to stagger seams continuously.

Verify: The visual preview shows a solid panel covering the studs, and the 3D view confirms the 12mm thickness is applied to the exterior face.

docs.title: Align studs to sheet splits (6:51)
docs.text:
Goal: Ensure there is always a stud positioned directly behind a vertical seam in the OSB.

Steps:

  1. Select Zone 0 in the zone list → the core layer properties appear.
  2. Type 1 in the Rely On field → the stud distribution recalculates to factor in Zone 1.

Verify: In the preview, an extra stud automatically generates exactly behind every vertical split in the exterior sheeting.

docs.title: Add interior sheet distribution (7:27)
docs.text:
Goal: Mirror the exterior sheathing setup to close off the interior side of the wall.

Steps:

  1. Click the + (add zone) button below Zone 0 → Zone -1 is created on the interior side.
  2. Select Sheet Distribution from the Zone filler dropdown → the sheeting properties appear.
  3. Select OSB from the Material dropdown → the OSB sheeting is applied to the inside face.
  4. Check the Continuously staggered box in the Distribution panel → the interior sheets stagger.
  5. Type OSB 12 in the Description fields for both Zone 1 and Zone -1 → the layers are clearly labeled.

Verify: The 3D preview shows the structural core sandwiched between two layers of 12mm OSB.

docs.title: Duplicate and modify for interior walls (8:07)
docs.text:
Goal: Quickly create a thinner interior wall template by copying and adjusting your finished exterior style.

Steps:

  1. Select the E1 - OSB_Stud184_OSB style in the sidebar → the style is highlighted.
  2. Click the copy icon and drag the duplicated style into the Wall - Interior Walls group → the style is duplicated into the new category.
  3. Type I1 - OSB_Stud89_OSB in the Name field → the interior style is renamed.
  4. Click the Inventory tab → the material mapping appears.
  5. Select 38x89 from the Default Beam dropdown → the horizontal plates resize to the narrower depth.
  6. Select 38x89 from the Studs alias dropdown in the inventory list → the vertical studs resize to match the plates.
  7. Click the Zones tab → the zone properties appear.
  8. Type OSB_38x89_OSB in the Description field → the description reflects the new dimensions.

Verify: Zooming into the top preview shows that the top plate perfectly matches the narrower 89mm studs.

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text:
• Unmatched plate and stud sizes — If your studs hang over the edge of your top or bottom plates, ensure you have set the Default Beam in the Inventory tab to exactly match the material mapped to your Studs alias.
  • Floating sheet splits — If you change the width of your sheeting material and your studs do not align with the seams, you must set the core zone to Rely on the sheet zone (e.g., Zone 0 relies on Zone 1).

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text: • Add corner and T-junction definitions in the Edge Details editor.

docs.title: Stretching wall sheets using edge details
docs.text:
Video info

Source: Watch on YouTube Duration: 3:28 Level: Intermediate

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Learn how to use edge details to fix sheathing sheets (like OSB) that do not extend fully to the top and bottom of your timber frame walls. You will also learn how to create detail configurations, allowing you to easily swap between different parametric variations—such as a single or double base plate—without building separate details.

docs.title: What you'll build
docs.text: You will create top and bottom edge details using the Cut tool to stretch the sheathing sheet across the full height of the wall. You will also add a parametric configuration to the bottom detail so you can toggle the second base plate on and off.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Knowledge: Basic familiarity with the Framing Styles Editor.
  • Project state: A Revit model with an generated HSBcad wall where the exterior sheathing sheets fall short of the top and bottom structural plates.

docs.title: Key concepts
docs.text:
• Framing styles editor — The interface in HSBcad where wall framing styles and their connection details are defined. Open it from the HSBcad ribbon.
  • Edge detail — A detail that handles what happens at the top and bottom of a sheet within a framing style.
  • Beam code — A short code (for example CD, CDS) assigned to elements in a detail to identify their type or function.
  • Generate — The HSBcad command that applies the current framing styles and details to the selected model elements and produces the actual timber-frame construction.
  • Construction — The set of framed wall elements (studs, plates, sheets, connectors) produced by the Generate command.
  • Yes/No parameter — A user-defined boolean parameter used to toggle elements or behaviours in a detail on and off.
  • Cut — An auxiliary geometry tool inside a detail that stretches or trims an element (a beam or sheet) by targeting its beam code.
  • Configuration — A named, saved snapshot of all parameter values inside a detail. Configurations let you switch between design variants without rebuilding the detail.

docs.title: Chapters
docs.text: Time What you'll do 0:00 Introduction 0:20 Creating the top edge detail 1:22 Creating the bottom edge detail 1:51 Adding configurations to the bottom detail 2:37 Generating the new construction

docs.title: Creating the top edge detail (0:20)
docs.text:
Goal: Open the framing styles editor and define a new detail that stretches the wall sheet up to the top plate.

Steps:

  1. Click Framing Styles Editor in the HSBcad ribbon → the editor dialog opens.
  2. Click the Edge Details tab for your target framing style → the edge details list appears.
  3. Click Add Detail under the top wall diagram → the detail editor opens with a default top edge detail.
  4. Select the horizontal top beam in the detail viewer → the Beam parameters panel appears.
  5. Type TP in the Beam code field → the beam code is updated to identify the top plate.
  6. Click Cut in the Tools menu on the Auxiliary Geometry tab → the cut tool activates.
  7. Click in the detail viewer directly above the wall → an upward-pointing arrow appears to indicate the stretch direction.
  8. Select the newly placed arrow → the Cut parameters panel appears.
  9. Type CDS in the Beam codes field → the cut tool now targets and stretches the sheathing sheet.
  10. Type W_Top in the Name field inside the Detail Template panel → the detail is renamed.
  11. Click OK → the detail is saved and you return to the main edge details list.

Verify: The W_Top detail is now listed in the top position of the edge details menu.

docs.title: Creating the bottom edge detail (1:22)
docs.text:
Goal: Create a complementary detail for the base of the wall to stretch the sheet downwards.

Steps:

  1. Click Add Detail under the bottom wall diagram in the Edge Details tab → the detail editor opens for the bottom edge.
  2. Click Cut in the Tools menu on the Auxiliary Geometry tab → the cut tool activates.
  3. Click in the detail viewer below the wall → a downward-pointing arrow appears.
  4. Select the downward arrow → the Cut parameters panel appears.
  5. Type CDS in the Beam codes field → the tool is configured to stretch the sheathing sheet downwards.

Verify: A downward-facing cut arrow is placed below the base plate, carrying the CDS beam code.

docs.title: Adding configurations to the bottom detail (1:51)
docs.text:
Goal: Create a parameter to toggle a second base plate on and off, then save both variations as reusable configurations.

Steps:

  1. Click Add yes/no parameter in the Parameters panel → a new parameter appears.
  2. Type No Second Beam into the parameter name field → the parameter is renamed.
  3. Select the bottom-most horizontal beam in the detail viewer → the Beam parameters panel appears.
  4. Check the box next to Set width to 0 and select No Second Beam from the adjacent dropdown menu → the parameter now controls whether the beam has a physical width.
  5. Check the box for No Second Beam in the Parameters panel → the second beam collapses and disappears from the detail viewer.
  6. Click Add configuration (the + icon) in the Configurations panel and type Single Beam → the one-beam state is saved as a new configuration.
  7. Click Add configuration again and type Two Beams → a second configuration is added.
  8. Uncheck the No Second Beam box while the Two Beams configuration is active → the second base plate reappears in the viewer.
  9. Click OK → the detail editor closes.
  10. Click OK in the main Framing Styles Editor dialog → your changes are saved to the project.

Verify: Back in the main editor dialog before clicking OK, the bottom edge detail displays both the Single Beam and Two Beams configurations in a dropdown underneath it.

docs.title: Generating the new construction (2:37)
docs.text:
Goal: Apply the updated framing style to the model so the sheets span the full height of the wall.

Steps:

  1. Select the target wall in the Revit model → the wall is highlighted.
  2. Click Generate in the HSBcad ribbon → the framing is rebuilt and the sheathing sheet extends fully to the top and bottom plates.

Verify: The visual gap between the sheathing sheet edges and the top/bottom plates in the 3D model is completely gone.

Warning

If the sheathing does not update successfully on the first try, select the wall, click Remove Construction in the HSBcad ribbon to clear the old framing, and then click Generate again.

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text: • Construction does not reflect detail changes — Sometimes Revit caches the old construction state. Select the wall, click Remove Construction, and click Generate again to force a clean rebuild.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text: • Configuring opening details for windows and doors.

docs.title: HSBcad terms used
docs.text:
Click any term to jump to its full definition in the glossary.

From the glossary:

docs.title: Match framing styles and generate item containers
docs.text:
Video info

Source: Watch on YouTube Duration: 6:18 Level: Beginner

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: You will link your predefined framing styles to Revit walls and create item containers. These containers define the boundaries for your timber-frame walls and let you generate the final construction geometry efficiently.

docs.title: What you'll build
docs.text: You'll map framing styles to your Revit walls, generate item containers, and sequentially number them. Finally, you will generate the 3D framing and learn how to lock containers to protect them from unintended changes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Knowledge: None.
  • Project state: A Revit model containing drawn walls, doors, and windows, along with predefined framing styles.

docs.title: Key concepts
docs.text:
• Framing style — A reusable template that defines the structure of a wall — the layout of its studs, plates, sheets, and other elements. Walls in the model are built from one or more framing styles.
  • Match framing styles — The HSBcad command that links Revit wall types to specific framing styles, including alignment (interior, center, exterior) and offset. The mapping is saved with the project so newly drawn walls of those types pick up the right framing automatically.
  • Item container — A logical boundary placed on a Revit wall that tells HSBcad which portion of the wall to frame. Item containers are the unit of selection for Generate, lock, and renumber operations — without one on a wall, HSBcad cannot produce a construction for it.
  • Model group — A named collection of item containers that can be managed, filtered, or generated together as a single unit — useful for grouping all walls of one storey or one building section.
  • Generate — The HSBcad command that applies the current framing styles and details to the selected model elements and produces the actual timber-frame construction. Found on the HSBcad ribbon.
  • Construction — The set of framed wall elements (studs, plates, sheets, connectors) produced by the Generate command from a framing style or details.

docs.title: Chapters
docs.text: Time What you'll do 0:34 Match framing styles to Revit walls 1:28 Create item containers 1:51 Renumber item containers dynamically 3:14 Generate the construction 4:03 Lock and unlock item containers 5:25 Flip item container orientation

docs.title: Match framing styles to Revit walls (0:34)
docs.text:
Goal: Assign specific framing styles to the interior and exterior wall types in your project.

Steps:

  1. Click Match Framing Styles in the hsbStickFrame ribbon → the matching dialog opens.
  2. Select an interior wall type from the list on the left → the wall's properties appear on the right.
  3. Select your predefined interior framing style from the HSB Framing Style drop-down → the style is assigned to the wall type.
  4. Click Exterior, Interior, or Center in the Alignment section → the zone alignment updates.
  5. Type a value in the Offset field if your Revit wall width differs from the framing style width → the offset is applied so the frame aligns correctly to one side.
  6. Repeat the process for your exterior walls, assigning the exterior framing style → the assignment is made.
  7. Click Save → the matched framing styles are saved to the project.

Verify: Your specific framing styles are firmly linked to the Revit wall types and ready for container generation.

docs.title: Create item containers (1:28)
docs.text:
Goal: Place item containers on all walls so HSBcad knows where to generate the framing.

Steps:

  1. Click Add Item Containers in the hsbStickFrame ribbon → the command activates.
  2. Drag a selection box over all walls in the model → the walls are highlighted.
  3. Click Finish in the options bar → item containers are added to every selected wall.

Verify: Item container icons appear on each wall in the model, and initial default names (like I1) populate automatically.

docs.title: Renumber item containers dynamically (1:51)
docs.text:
Goal: Assign logical prefixes and sequential numbers to your item containers to easily identify them.

Steps:

  1. Click the drop-down under Item Containers in the hsbStickFrame ribbon and select Item Container Renumber → the Dynamic Renumber dialog opens.
  2. Type E in the Prefix field to designate exterior walls → the prefix updates.
  3. Type 1 in the Start Number field → the sequence is ready to start at E1.
  4. Click Select item 1 by one in the Pick Objects section → the selection mode is set.
  5. Click OK → the dialog closes and the command activates.
  6. Click the exterior walls one by one in the order you want them numbered → each container label updates sequentially (E1, E2, E3...) upon selection.
  7. Press Enter on your keyboard → the command finishes.
  8. Repeat this sequence using the prefix I to number all your interior walls.

Verify: Each wall possesses a clearly labeled item container (e.g., E1 through E6 for exterior walls, I1 through I4 for interior walls).

docs.title: Generate the construction (3:14)
docs.text:
Goal: Build the physical 3D framing elements inside the assigned item containers.

Steps:

  1. Click Generate in the hsbStickFrame ribbon → the command activates.
  2. Drag a selection box over all item containers in the model → the containers are highlighted.
  3. Click Finish in the options bar → a progress bar appears, and the 3D timber construction generates inside the walls.

Verify: The wooden studs, plates, and sheathing are now fully visible in your 3D view.

docs.title: Lock and unlock item containers (4:03)
docs.text:
Goal: Protect specific item containers from being regenerated when making sweeping changes to the rest of the model.

Steps:

  1. Click Lock Item Containers in the hsbStickFrame ribbon → the tool activates.
  2. Click the item container you want to protect → the container highlights.
  3. Press Enter on your keyboard → the selected item container turns red.
  4. Click Unlock Item Containers in the hsbStickFrame ribbon to reverse the process → the tool activates.
  5. Click the red item container and press Enter on your keyboard → the container returns to its normal color.

Verify: The locked item container is visually distinct (red) and will successfully ignore any global Generate commands.

Tip

You can also lock or unlock an item container directly from the Properties panel. Select the container and check or uncheck the Locked property.

docs.title: Flip item container orientation (5:25)
docs.text:
Goal: Correct the interior/exterior orientation of an item container so the framing generates on the right side.

Steps:

  1. Click an item container in the model view → its properties display in the Properties panel.
  2. Click the flip icon (double arrows) floating near the selected container → the container's orientation flips to the opposite side.

Verify: The icon indicates the item container boundary has inverted its interior and exterior sides.

Warning

If you flip an item container after the construction has already been generated, the physical framing will become out of sync with the container's new orientation. You will need to regenerate the wall to fix the alignment.
